# Buick Lacrosse CXL Transmission Fluid Compatibility: Dexron III vs. Dexron VI

The specific question regarding your Buick LaCrosse CXL centers on a common friction point in automotive maintenance: the transition from Dexron III to Dexron VI. The shop performed the service using an STP brand fluid labeled as Dexron III, yet official General Motors documentation recommends Dexron VI for this model year and higher. While you are correct that GM officially shifted its stance to Dexron VI around 2010â2011, the short answer is that switching your transmission from a Dexron III fill to a Dexron VI fluid will not damage your unit.

This compatibility stems from the fundamental chemical relationship between the two fluids. Dexron VI is not a different type of lubricant; it is an upgrade in performance characteristics built upon the same base chemistry as Dexron III. GM developed Dexron VI specifically to maintain backward compatibility with existing transmissions while improving efficiency and shift quality. The molecular structure allows Dexron VI to function seamlessly within systems originally designed for Dexron III, provided you are not performing a "flush" where old fluid is completely drained and replaced with the new specification without considering viscosity shifts.

In terms of implementation, think of this like updating a dependency in a legacy codebase. You can run your application on the latest version of a library (Dexron VI) even if it was written for an older version (Dexron III), because the API surface remains compatible and often backward-compatible features are preserved. However, mixing them or using the wrong viscosity during a full flush is where risks emerge. If you drain 100% of the old fluid and fill entirely with Dexron VI, the transmission will operate under improved thermal management conditions, effectively upgrading its performance envelope without causing harm.

The potential pitfalls usually arise not from the fluid specification itself, but from how the change is executed. A critical error occurs when a technician attempts to "flush" an older transmission that has been running on Dexron III for thousands of miles by using a high-pressure machine. These machines often force a volume of fluid that exceeds the factory fill capacity (typically 10-12 quarts for many GM automatics). If you overfill the system with Dexron VI, the increased hydraulic pressure can cause clutches to slip prematurely or overwhelm the torque converter lock-up logic. Conversely, if you are topping off a drained vehicle and accidentally add Dexron III to a system now filled with Dexron VI, the mixture will still function because Dexron VI contains the necessary additives to tolerate the older base oil, but the result is suboptimal friction modification performance.

It is also worth noting that STP branding on the bottle indicates the manufacturer of the additive package or the distributor, not necessarily the fluid chemistry itself. As long as the label explicitly states "Dexron III" and meets GM's MS-9793 specification, it is a valid fill for your LaCrosse CXL. However, if you are looking to align with modern best practices and potentially improve fuel economy or shift smoothness, switching to a certified Dexron VI fluid is the safer long-term choice. This approach ensures you are utilizing the latest friction modifiers designed to handle the higher torque loads common in modern drivetrains.

For developers managing fleet vehicles or maintaining legacy systems, the lesson is clear: backward compatibility is usually preserved in engineering updates. You do not need to panic about a service performed with Dexron III, but you should plan for a future switch to Dexron VI when you are ready for an oil change, ensuring you use a gravity drain or low-pressure exchange method rather than a high-pressure flush until the system has had time to adapt to the new viscosity standards.
